title_original: Libraryman : François Halard : Conversation with Claude

blocks.text: Is photography a language? One might think so, since anyone can express themselves through it. Yet an image does not speak, though it is not mute either. It gives us something to see (and therefore to think about). It says things, but its language is coded, and to decipher it one must pay attention to the elements that make it up. Once the observer has moved beyond passive viewing, an exchange becomes far more likely.

Photography reveals itself, and the sensibility of the beholder can project itself into it through the light present, its contrasts, the harmony of colors, the nuances of black and white, the importance given in the framing to certain elements or not… or the instant chosen to freeze the moment. All of these signs matter and give meaning.

Thus a silent dialogue takes hold: the artist’s technical and aesthetic choices can be interpreted by the viewer through the signs on display, and a space for discussion can emerge. This conversation seems to be a meeting point between an artist’s intention and its reception as interpreted by a viewer.

In photographing Monet’s gardens at Giverny, François Halard was not content to bring back a series of Polaroids. He set about adding paint to enlargements of the original snapshots, either in delicate, speckled touches or in a dripping manner, which seem to ooze from the surface of the images. Since Polaroids already have a chance-driven, even impressionistic, definition, the second, painted stage seems to give material form to this exchange of gazes.

In revealing these hybrid works to us in the beautiful book “ Conversation with Claude ,” or on the stand of the Ruttkowski;68 gallery at Paris Photo, Halard was not trying to document his stay; he too, just like Claude Monet, offers a personal version of his contemplation of the landscape. Opera director Vincent Huguet, who wrote the introductory essay to the book, tells us: “ Each touch resembles the petal of a flower, at times with an impressionist lightness, at times with an expressionist energy recalling, in passing, that the lily pond was also one of the crucibles of American abstract painting. We find ourselves at once in a Japanese garden and in New York, in Normandy and in a studio in Arles. ”

More than a century later, François Halard has put himself in the position of interpreting the light, the waters and the vegetation, and, through a figurative-abstract technique, of playing with reflections and blurs, to deliver his singular and intimate conversation with Impressionism. Photography and its reality blend with the sensitive signs of painting, giving concrete form to the idea of an active exchange between the one who first drew the splashes and the contemporary eye that revives its memory.

“Conversation with Claude” by François Halard, published November 1 by Tony Cederteg/Libraryman. https://libraryman.se/ . The works will be presented in a solo show by the Ruttkowski;68 gallery on the occasion of Paris Photo 2026. Info: https://www.ruttkowski68.com/exhibition/conversation-with-claude/
